teach.title: What it does

notice.ask: Tap the verb at the end of each sentence. What do the two endings have in common?

teach.say: The subjunctive of a finished action is **the perfect subjunctive (the 'have done' form: nesciō quid fēcerit; nē timuerīs = don't be afraid)**. A present subjunctive says what is going on, the perfect what has been done: *nesciō quid faciat*, I don't know what he is doing; *nesciō quid fēcerit*, what he has done.

check.ask: Rogō is present. Does fēcerit say what Marcus is doing, or what he has done?

teach.title: The singular: perfect stem + -erim, -erīs, -erit
teach.say: Take the perfect stem, the third principal part without its *-ī* (*fēcī → fēc-*, *vēnī → vēn-*), and add **-erim** for 'I', **-erīs** for 'you', **-erit** for 'he, she, it': *fēcerim, fēcerīs, fēcerit*. The *-erī-* is long in *-erīs, -erīmus, -erītis*, and short in *-erim, -erit, -erint*.

check.ask: Fill the three singular perfect subjunctive forms of scrībō.

teach.title: The plural: -erīmus, -erītis, -erint
teach.say: The plural adds **-erīmus**, **-erītis**, **-erint** to the same stem: *fēcerīmus, fēcerītis, fēcerint*. So *cessāvī* gives *cessāverint* and *vīdī* gives *vīderint*. One stem, six endings.

check.ask: Now the three plural perfect subjunctive forms of scrībō.

teach.title: Not the future perfect
teach.say: The two share almost every letter. *fēcerō, fēceris, fēcerit* is the future perfect (the 'will have done' tense) and states a plain fact; *fēcerim, fēcerīs, fēcerit* is the subjunctive and sits inside a folded question or after *cum*. Since *-erit* and *-erint* are spelled the same in both, the clause around the verb decides.

check.ask: frēgerit: future perfect indicative, or perfect subjunctive?

teach.title: nē with this form means 'don't'
teach.say: A second and quite different use: *nē* with the perfect subjunctive in the second person is an ordinary way of saying 'don't'. *Nē timuerīs* — don't be afraid. *Nē hoc vīnum biberīs* — don't drink this wine. To more than one person: *nē cucurrerītis* — don't run.

check.ask: nē with biberīs: is this a wish, a question, or 'don't'?

teach.title: Use it
teach.say: After a present verb of asking, knowing or wondering, put the finished action into the perfect subjunctive: *nescit quid fīlius ēmerit*. When the verb is passive it is two words, the perfect participle with *sim, sīs, sit*: *nesciō ā quō epistula scrīpta sit*.

check.ask: Nescit is present. Put emō into the perfect subjunctive.

core.text: For something already completed when the main verb is present, the subjunctive (the form Latin uses for wishes, purposes and what someone tells someone to do) becomes **the perfect subjunctive (the 'have done' form: nescio quid fecerit; ne timueris = don't be afraid)**: *nesciō quid fēcerit* — I don't know what he did. Forms: perfect stem + *-erim, -eris (-erīs), -erit, -erimus, -eritis, -erint*; passive: perfect participle + *sim, sīs, sit* (*captus sit*). *nē* + perfect subjunctive is a sharp 'don't': *nē timuerīs!* Latin name: *coniūnctīvus perfectī*.
English 'did' in a report: *I wonder why you didn't tell me*. The telling is earlier than the wondering; Latin marks that gap.
Present main verb + a finished action in the clause → perfect subjunctive. nē + perfect subjunctive = don't (like nōlī + infinitive).

invented.en: I ask what the boy said.

core.text: Same endings except the first singular (*-erim* against *-erō*). The job decides: *sī vēnerit, gaudēbō* looks ahead to a future event — the future perfect (the 'will have done' tense); *nesciō an vēnerit* reports a past one; *nē vēnerīs* forbids. Signals for the subjunctive: *nē*, or a question word after a verb of knowing or asking.

more.text: Also easy to confuse: two ways to say 'don't' — *nōlī* + infinitive (*nōlī timēre*), gentle and the usual one in prose; *nē* + perfect subjunctive (*nē timuerīs*), brisker. Both are orders, not wishes. The second person is *-eris* in the grammars but *-erīs* in Ørberg and the poets; both are attested, and this course prints the long one in examples.

The learner's notes: the perfect subjunctive replaces the present whenever a sense of completion is needed; 2nd stem + *-eri-* + the plain endings *-m, -s, -t, -mus, -tis, -nt* (*cēperim*); passive from the 3rd stem + *sim, sīs, sit* (*captus sim*). It appears in wishes and 'might' statements, but mostly after causal *cum* and in indirect questions: *nōn possum exīre cum aliquis portam clauserit* (I cannot go out since someone has shut the gate); *dīc mihi quandō advēnerīs!*; *sciō quandō nātus sīs* (I know when you were born).

Ørberg's chapter 32: *Iūlius dubitat num magister Mārcum laudāverit* — the doubting is now, the praising was earlier; *pater dubitat num fīlius laudātus sit*; and the prohibition *nē dubitāverīs dē verbīs meīs!* Irregulars: *fuerim, potuerim, voluerim, ierim*. In the sequence of tenses the perfect subjunctive is the 'before' partner of the present subjunctive; after a past main verb its place is taken by the pluperfect subjunctive (Week 12).
In a folded question the perfect subjunctive follows a main verb in the present (*nesciō quid fēcerit*); it is the tense for what was finished before the asking.
*-erit* and *-erint* are spelled the same in both tenses, and *-eris/-erīs*, *-erimus/-erīmus*, *-eritis/-erītis* differ only in the length of the i, so the clause around the verb decides.
